Oh, constantly. It's like my brain just won't shut off. My mind just keeps jumping all over the place. Well, yeah, I suppose it is. I've actually started falling behind on my lesson prep and grading lately. It just takes me forever to get through a stack of essays now. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Control it? No. No, not really. I mean, I try. I can tell myself to stop, you know, take a breath and just focus on the class in front of me. But then one small thought pops in—like, I'll remember an unpaid invoice for the theater, or I'll notice a student falling behind. Like Tommy in my third period. He used to be such a bright kid, always had his hand up, but lately he just stares out the window. I tried talking to his mother at parent-teacher conferences, but she was more interested in complaining about the new traffic light they put in on Elm Street. Which, to be fair, is a disaster. It stays red for a solid three minutes, even when there's no cross traffic. I timed it once when I was stuck there behind a garbage truck. The smell was just awful. It was middle of August, 90 degrees out, and this truck was just baking in the sun... 

But yeah, anyway, if I have a thought like that—about Tommy, or the invoice—it just sets off this whole chain of what-ifs. And once that chain starts, I just can't shut it down. It just keeps going and going.

Headaches or stomach problems? No, not really. My stomach's always been pretty ironclad. Though, I tell you, the new food vendor they brought into the school cafeteria this year is doing their absolute best to test that. They serve this... I don't even know what it is. Worse than most people? I... I don't know. Maybe? I mean, I feel like my mind just never stops. It just keeps jumping around. Susan actually baked three dozen of her famous snickerdoodles for it. \n\nBut yeah, it just cycles like that. No, I wouldn't say sad. Just... wound up, I guess. I mean, I don't sit around crying or feeling hopeless or anything like that. It was making me sick to my stomach trying to juggle it all. \n\nWhich is a real shame, because the theater group is usually my escape, you know? We've got this new director this season, a young woman named Chloe, just moved here from Chicago. She's got all these avant-garde ideas. She wanted to do a modern adaptation of *Hamlet* where everyone is on roller skates. Can you imagine? I mean, the liability insurance alone would bankrupt us. I tried explaining that to her, but she just kept talking about \"kinetic energy\" and \"spatial dynamics.\" I don't know where they find these people. I think she used to work at a coffee shop before this. One of those fancy places where they take ten minutes to pour hot water over grounds and charge you eight bucks for it. I went into one of those places once, over by the university, and asked for a regular black coffee. You'd think I asked them to sacrifice a goat right there on the counter. The barista gave me this look... \n\nBut, uh, anyway. Yeah. The worrying is definitely taking a toll. I just feel like I can't keep all the plates spinning anymore, you know?\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you're able to control your worrying most of the time?\n\nPatient: Control it? No. No, not really. I mean, I try. I can tell myself to stop, you know, take a breath and just focus on the class in front of me. But then one small thought pops in—like, I'll remember an unpaid invoice for the theater, or I'll notice a student falling behind. Like Tommy in my third period. He used to be such a bright kid, always had his hand up, but lately he just stares out the window. I tried talking to his mother at parent-teacher conferences, but she was more interested in complaining about the new traffic light they put in on Elm Street. Which, to be fair, is a disaster. It stays red for a solid three minutes, even when there's no cross traffic. I timed it once when I was stuck there behind a garbage truck. The smell was just awful. It was middle of August, 90 degrees out, and this truck was just baking in the sun... \n\nBut yeah, anyway, if I have a thought like that—about Tommy, or the invoice—it just sets off this whole chain of what-ifs. And once that chain starts, I just can't shut it down. It just keeps going and going.\n\nDoctor: Have you been avoiding certain situations or activities because of your worrying?\n\nPatient: Avoid? No, I wouldn't say I avoid things, not exactly. I still go to work, I still do my grocery shopping. Well, mostly. I did stop going to the big supermarket on the weekends because it's just a madhouse. The aisles are so narrow, and they have those massive displays of soda right in the middle where you're trying to turn your cart. Last month, this woman with three kids just plowed right into one of those displays. Cans everywhere. Diet cola spraying all over the linoleum. And did the kids help pick it up? Of course not. They were too busy staring at their phones. I swear, this generation is going to have permanent neck damage from looking down all the time. My chiropractor, Dr. Evans, he was telling me he's seeing kids as young as twelve coming in with spinal issues. Twelve! When I was twelve, I was outside riding my bike until the streetlights came on. We used to build these ramps out of scrap wood we found behind the old lumber yard...\n\nBut no, I don't really avoid things because of the worrying. I just... I might drag my feet a bit, or dread doing them, but I still show up. I just feel awful the whole time.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any other physical symptoms, such as headaches or stomach issues, alongside the muscle tightness?\n\nPatient: Headaches or stomach problems? No, not really. My stomach's always been pretty ironclad. Though, I tell you, the new food vendor they brought into the school cafeteria this year is doing their absolute best to test that. They serve this... I don't even know what it is. It's supposed to be Salisbury steak, I think, but it looks like a wet kitchen sponge. \n\nI was talking to Dan, the biology teacher, about it the other day. Dan's been teaching there almost as long as I have, maybe twenty-five years now. He actually took a sample of the cafeteria gravy and put it under a microscope in his third-period lab. He used to have this huge iguana in his classroom named Sir Isaac, but he had to take it home because the new principal decided it was some sort of health hazard. I don't know if other people worry this much, but it feels like a lot to carry around all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is affecting your relationships with your family or friends?\n\nPatient: Affecting my relationships? Um, well, I'm not entirely sure. I don't think it's pushing anyone away, exactly. But, you know, Sarah... she's a saint, really. She notices when I'm wound up. Like last Friday, we were supposed to go over to our friends' house, the Millers. We've known them since college. Tom Miller and I actually lived in the same dorm, second floor of Henderson Hall. That building was a disaster even back then. The heating never worked right, so we'd all have our windows open in January while the radiators hissed and banged all night. Tom used to have this huge collection of vinyl records—mostly classic rock, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd—and he'd play them so loud the RA would come down at least twice a week to yell at us. Suddenly it's in absolutely everything. You can't even go to a diner and get a regular side salad anymore without it being full of these bitter, tough leaves. My sister tried to make kale chips for Thanksgiving last year, and they tasted like salted paper... \n\nBut, uh, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my stomach. No, my stomach is fine. And no headaches either, thankfully. Just that tightness in my shoulders and back that I mentioned.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your worrying is worse than what most people would worry about in the same situations?\n\nPatient: Worse than most people? I... I don't know. Maybe? I mean, I feel like my mind just never stops. It just keeps jumping around. One minute I'm agonizing over whether the contractors missed something when they were fixing the roof last month. Which, by the way, was a complete nightmare. They said it would take three days, and they were there for two and a half weeks. Two and a half weeks of hammering starting at 7 AM! And the dust... it got everywhere. My wife, Sarah, she was so patient about it, but I could tell it was wearing on her. She's been so busy lately anyway with her new job at the library. They've got her doing all this community outreach, setting up these reading programs for toddlers. It's wonderful work, really, but the budget they give her is practically non-existent. She was telling me the other night that she had to buy construction paper out of her own pocket just so the kids could make these little caterpillar crafts...\n\nBut anyway, my mind just goes from the house repairs, to whether my lesson plans are slipping, to whether the robotics kids are falling behind. We have a competition coming up in three weeks, and the drive train on our main bot keeps stalling. I told them we needed to switch to a different gear ratio, but you know teenagers, they want to do it their way. Which I respect, I really do, but it's just one more thing keeping me up at night. And then I start worrying that I'm disappointing Sarah and the rest of the family by not keeping everything under control. It's just... it's exhausting. I don't know if other people worry this much, but it feels like a lot to carry around all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is affecting your relationships with your family or friends?\n\nPatient: Affecting my relationships? Um, well, I'm not entirely sure. I don't think it's pushing anyone away, exactly. But, you know, Sarah... she's a saint, really. She notices when I'm wound up. Like last Friday, we were supposed to go over to our friends' house, the Millers. We've known them since college. Tom Miller and I actually lived in the same dorm, second floor of Henderson Hall. That building was a disaster even back then. The heating never worked right, so we'd all have our windows open in January while the radiators hissed and banged all night. Tom used to have this huge collection of vinyl records—mostly classic rock, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd—and he'd play them so loud the RA would come down at least twice a week to yell at us. The RA was this pre-med guy, super intense, always walking around with a clipboard... \n\nAnyway, we were supposed to go over to Tom and Linda's for dinner, and I was just so exhausted from worrying all week about the robotics team and the roof and everything else, I just kind of sat on the couch staring at the wall. Sarah asked if I was okay, and I just couldn't even muster the energy to explain it all again. So I guess she ends up carrying a lot of the conversational weight when we go out. But, I don't know if that means it's affecting the relationship in a bad way. I just... I don't really know how much it bothers her.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of distress?\n\nPatient: Distress? Um... I don't know if I'd call it distress, exactly. I mean, I guess I'm not entirely sure. It's definitely tiring, that's for sure. \n\nSpeaking of tiring, I was up half the night on Tuesday grading these sophomore physics labs. The handwriting on some of these kids... I have this one student, Kevin, and he writes like he's gripping the pen with his entire fist. I tried to bring it up to his mother at the parent-teacher conferences last week. They held them in the gymnasium this year instead of the classrooms, which was just a terrible idea. The acoustics in there are absolutely awful, it just echoes everyone's conversations, and it always smells like floor wax and old gym socks. \n\nThe head custodian, Mr. Higgins, uses this industrial wax that is just so incredibly strong. He's actually retiring next month, though, after thirty years at the school. They're throwing a potluck for him in the teachers' lounge next Friday. I really need to remember to chip in for his gift... Sarah usually reminds me about those things, she's got a memory like a steel trap. She remembered her cousin's anniversary last week and even mailed them a physical card. I haven't bought a stamp in probably five years. The post office in our town moved, too, over by the old strip mall... \n\nBut, um, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Distress? Right. Yeah, I don't know. I haven't really thought of it as distress, or noticed it being that severe. It's mostly just... a lot going on up here, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed your worrying and tension affecting your relationships or daily activities consistently over the past seven months?\n\nPatient: Consistently over the past seven months? Well, I mean... yeah, it's definitely been affecting things. Like, I've actually started falling behind on my lesson prep and my grading, which I hate. I've always prided myself on having my grades posted by Monday morning. My first year teaching, my mentor, Mrs. Gable—she taught earth science—she drilled that into my head. She'd say, \"The kids need the feedback while it's fresh.\" She was this tiny woman, couldn't have been more than five feet tall, but she commanded that classroom like a general. She had this incredible collection of geodes on her desk. She actually gave me a piece of amethyst when she retired. I still have it on my bookshelf at home, right next to this old copy of *The Lord of the Rings* that my dad gave me when I was twelve. The binding is completely falling apart on that book, I really should get it repaired... there's a bookbinder downtown, near that bakery that makes those incredible almond croissants. Sarah and I used to go there on Sunday mornings before they changed their hours... \n\nBut anyway, yeah, the grading is piling up. And I actually had to give up some of the community theater work I usually manage. I usually do the set design for the spring musical, but I just... I couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. It was just too much. I felt terrible telling the director, but I was just so wound up all the time.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your worrying is out of proportion to the actual problems you're facing?\n\nPatient: Out of proportion? Um... I don't know, honestly. I mean, the problems are real, right? The roof really is leaking, and the robotics team really does need funding. \n\nSpeaking of the robotics team, we actually have a competition coming up in three weeks. It's the regional qualifier, over in the next county. We have to take a bus, and I always get nervous about the bus company the school uses. Last year, the heater on the bus broke on the way back, and it was freezing. The kids were all huddled under their coats. One of my students, Chloe, she had this massive puffy jacket that looked like a sleeping bag. She's such a bright girl, she wants to go to MIT for engineering. Her older brother went there, actually. He came back to visit the school last year and gave a little talk to my physics class. He works for some aerospace company now, designing satellite components or something. It sounded fascinating, but I couldn't quite follow all the technical jargon he was using. It made me realize how much the field has changed since I got my degree. I got my bachelor's back in '91, and computers were barely a thing in the classroom then. We used to have to type out our papers on these heavy electric typewriters. My roommate had this Smith Corona that hummed so loudly... \n\nBut, um, you were asking if my worrying is out of proportion? I'm not really sure. I guess I haven't really thought about it like that. I just know there's a lot to worry about, and I just... worry about it.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble sleeping due to your worrying?\n\nPatient: Trouble sleeping? Well, I mean, sometimes, yeah. But I don't know if it's always the worrying that keeps me up. Sometimes I just can't fall asleep. \n\nLike last night, I was lying there and I kept hearing this weird tapping noise outside the window. We have this old oak tree in the front yard, and I think one of the branches has grown too close to the house. I really need to get someone out to trim it before the winter storms hit. Last winter, we had that terrible ice storm that knocked out the power for three days. Sarah and I had to drag all our perishables out to the garage just to keep them cold. We ended up eating cold beans out of a can by candlelight. It was actually kind of romantic, in a way. We used these beeswax candles that we bought at a craft fair up in Vermont a few years ago. We try to go up there every autumn to see the leaves change, but we missed it this year because the car was acting up. The transmission started making this awful grinding sound whenever I shifted into third gear. I took it to my mechanic, Tony—he's got this shop over on Elm Street, right next to that diner that serves breakfast all day. I love a good diner breakfast. There's nothing quite like a stack of pancakes at two in the afternoon...\n\nBut, sorry, sleep. Right. Um, I guess I'm not really sure if it's the worrying specifically that's keeping me awake. I just... I don't sleep great, generally speaking. I haven't really noticed a direct connection, I suppose.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is causing you significant emotional pain or discomfort?\n\nPatient: Significant emotional pain? Um... I don't know if I'd call it pain, exactly. Discomfort, maybe? It's just... I'm just always wound up. \n\nSpeaking of being wound up, my sister's dog is like that. She has this little Jack Russell terrier named Buster, and he literally never stops moving. He just vibrates with energy. She brought him over for Thanksgiving last year, and he spent the entire afternoon chasing his own tail in the living room. He actually knocked over this antique floor lamp that belonged to my grandmother. It has this beautiful stained glass shade, kind of like a Tiffany lamp, but not a real one, obviously. My grandmother got it at an estate sale back in the seventies. She loved going to estate sales and antique shops. She had this whole collection of vintage salt and pepper shakers shaped like different animals. There was a pair of penguins that I always liked playing with when I was a kid. I used to pretend they were sliding down the mashed potatoes on my plate... \n\nBut, uh, emotional pain? I guess I haven't really thought of it like that. It's just exhausting, you know? Just feeling this way all the time. But I wouldn't say it's, like, severe pain or anything. I just... I don't know.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you've been worrying excessively about everyday things for more than six months?\n\nPatient: Excessively? Um, well... I guess it's been about seven months now. Yeah, right around then. It all started when that pipe burst in the upstairs bathroom. It completely ruined the ceiling in the dining room below it. We had to get contractors in, and the whole remodeling process just threw the house into total chaos. \n\nSpeaking of the contractors, the guy running the crew, Mike, he was a real character. He always wore these bright orange suspenders, every single day. Said they were his lucky suspenders because he bought them at a hardware store in Maine on a fishing trip where he caught a record-breaking bass. He actually showed me a picture of it on his phone. It was huge! He said he had it mounted and it's hanging in his den. I've never really been fishing myself. I tried it once when I was maybe twelve, at a summer camp in the Poconos, but I just ended up getting my line tangled in a tree branch. The camp counselor had to climb up and cut it loose. He wasn't very happy about it. That camp was something else, though. We had archery, and canoeing, and they made us do these trust falls... \n\nBut, right, the worrying. Yeah, it's been about seven months since the pipe burst and everything went crazy. So, I guess that's more than six months, yeah.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is making it hard for you to enjoy time with your family or perform your job as a teacher?\n\nPatient: Hard for me to enjoy time with my family or... or do my job? Well, yeah, it's definitely been affecting school. I've started falling behind on my lesson prep and grading, which is so unlike me. I usually have everything planned out a week in advance. \n\nI actually had to give up some of the community theater work I usually manage, too, because I just couldn't keep up with all of it anymore. It was just too much. I've been doing the set design for the local playhouse for years. We were supposed to do *Our Town* this spring, which is a classic, you know? The minimalist set is actually harder to pull off than you'd think because every little detail matters. You can't hide behind big, flashy backdrops. We did *The Music Man* last year, and I built this incredible gazebo for the town square scenes. I used real cedar wood so it would smell authentic. I got the wood from this lumberyard out on Route 9. The guy who runs it, Stan, he's been there forever. He has this old golden retriever that just sleeps under the counter all day. Sweetest dog. You can just pet him for hours and he won't even open his eyes. I always bring him a milk bone when I go in. Stan says he's getting arthritis in his hips, which is a shame. My neighbor's dog had that, and they got him this special ramp to get up into the car...\n\nBut, uh, anyway, yeah. The teaching and the theater... I just had to step back from the theater stuff. And grading has been a real struggle lately. I just can't seem to focus on it."
